descripcion_es: Rising, falling, levelling off; percentages and comparisons.
resumen: Verbs, nouns and adverbs for describing graphs and data: rises, falls, stability, highs and lows, percentages and percentage points.

explicacion.texto: Prepositions are key: “rise BY 2%” gives the amount of the change; “rise TO 5%” gives the final level; “FROM 3% TO 5%” gives the starting point and the end point. And don't confuse “percent” (porcentaje) with “percentage point” (punto porcentual).

filas: to rise / to increase / to go up
to become higher (es: subir, aumentar)
Sales rose by 10%.
to soar / to surge / to rocket
to rise very quickly and sharply (es: dispararse)
Energy prices soared last winter.
to climb / to pick up
to rise gradually / to recover (es: subir poco a poco / repuntar)
Demand picked up in spring.
to fall / to drop / to decline / to go down
to become lower (es: caer, bajar)
Unemployment fell to 11%.
to plunge / to plummet / to slump
to fall suddenly and steeply (es: desplomarse)
Shares plummeted after the news.
to level off / to stabilise
to stop rising or falling (es: estabilizarse)
Prices levelled off in June.
to remain stable / to hold steady
to stay at the same level (es: mantenerse estable)
The rate held steady at 2%.
to fluctuate
to go up and down irregularly (es: fluctuar, oscilar)
Oil prices fluctuated wildly.
to peak / to reach a peak
to reach the highest point (es: alcanzar un máximo)
Inflation peaked at 10.8%.
to hit a low / to bottom out
to reach the lowest point (es: tocar fondo)
The market bottomed out in March.
to double / to triple / to halve
to become two / three times as big; to become half as big (es: duplicarse / triplicarse / reducirse a la mitad)
Profits have doubled since 2020.
a sharp / steep rise
a sudden, large rise (es: una subida brusca)
There was a sharp rise in rents.
a slight / modest fall
a small fall (es: una ligera caída)
A slight fall in exports.
a steady / gradual increase
a regular, slow increase (es: un aumento constante / gradual)
A steady increase in tourism.
dramatically / significantly
by a large amount (es: drásticamente / considerablemente)
Costs rose dramatically.
slightly / marginally
by a small amount (es: ligeramente / mínimamente)
Output fell slightly.
percentage point
the absolute difference between two percentages (es: punto porcentual)
From 3% to 5% is a rise of two percentage points.
year-on-year / month-on-month
compared with the same period of the previous year / month (es: interanual / intermensual)
Prices rose 4% year-on-year.
twice as high as / three times as many
two / three times the amount of (es: el doble de / el triple de)
Rents are twice as high as in 2015.
roughly / approximately / just over / just under
about / a little more than / a little less than (es: aproximadamente / algo más de / algo menos de)
Just under half voted yes.
the figures / the data show
the numbers / the data show (es: las cifras / los datos muestran)
The latest figures show a recovery.

items: The verb “rise” (rose, risen) is intransitive; “raise” (raised) is transitive: “The bank raised rates”; “Rates rose”.
Decimals use a point: “2.5%” is read “two point five percent”.
Thousands take a comma: “1,500” = one thousand five hundred.

ejemplos.frase: House prices rose by 8% last year, the sharpest rise in a decade.
ejemplos.traduccion: El precio de la vivienda subió un 8% el año pasado, la mayor subida en una década.

ejemplos.frase: Unemployment fell from 14% to 11% over three years.
ejemplos.traduccion: El paro bajó del 14% al 11% en tres años.

ejemplos.frase: Ticket sales plummeted during the lockdown.
ejemplos.traduccion: La venta de entradas se desplomó durante el confinamiento.

ejemplos.frase: After months of growth, visitor numbers have levelled off.
ejemplos.traduccion: Tras meses de crecimiento, el número de visitantes se ha estabilizado.

ejemplos.frase: The number of cyclists in the city has almost tripled.
ejemplos.traduccion: El número de ciclistas en la ciudad casi se ha triplicado.

ejemplos.frase: Just over a third of students live with their parents.
ejemplos.traduccion: Algo más de un tercio de los estudiantes vive con sus padres.

errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Inflation increased by two percentage points.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: The amount of the change goes with “by”, and the difference between percentages is measured in percentage points.
The final level is introduced with “to”.
In English the decimal separator is a point and is read “point”.

ejercicios.frase: Sales ___ by 15% in the first quarter.
ejercicios.explicacion: The note in Rules and keys applies: rise (rose, risen) is intransitive, whereas raise (raised) is transitive and needs an object. The clue is that the subject, sales, goes up by itself and there is no direct object: by 15% only gives the amount of the change. So the correct past form is rose.
ejercicios.traduccion: Las ventas subieron un 15 % en el primer trimestre.

por_opcion.rose: Correct: irregular past of rise, intransitive; sales go up by themselves.
por_opcion.raised: Incorrect: raise is transitive (raise prices); without a direct object it doesn't work.
por_opcion.arose: Incorrect: arise means to come up or appear (a problem arose), not to go up.
por_opcion.rised: Incorrect: it doesn't exist; rise is irregular and its past is rose.

ejercicios.frase: The unemployment rate fell ___ 9% in May.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule on prepositions in this sheet applies: to gives the final level reached, whereas by would give the amount of the change. The clue is in the instruction (final level) and in the meaning: unemployment ended up at 9%, it did not fall by nine points. Fell to 9% is the equivalent of Spanish “bajó hasta el 9 %” or “se situó en el 9 %”.
ejercicios.traduccion: La tasa de paro bajó al 9 % en mayo.

por_opcion.to: Correct: to marks the final level reached.
por_opcion.by: Incorrect: by would give the amount of the fall (it fell by nine points), not the final level the instruction asks for.
por_opcion.until: Incorrect: until is about time (up to when); it is a literal translation of Spanish “hasta el 9 %”.
por_opcion.in: Incorrect: in gives neither amount nor level; in this sentence in already appears with the month (in May).

ejercicios.enunciado: Choose the correct preposition (amount of the change).
ejercicios.frase: Prices increased ___ 3% compared with last year.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule on prepositions in this sheet applies: by gives how much a quantity has changed. The clue is the instruction (amount of the change) and compared with last year, which shows that the variation is being measured. Increased by 3% is Spanish “aumentaron un 3 %”. Spanish speakers tend to write in, a literal translation of “en un 3 %”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “By” gives how much something has changed.
ejercicios.traduccion: Los precios subieron un 3 % respecto al año pasado.

por_opcion.by: Correct: by expresses the size of the change.
por_opcion.in: Incorrect: literal translation of Spanish “en un 3 %”; in English the amount of the change goes with by.
por_opcion.of: Incorrect: of is used with the noun (an increase of 3%), not with the verb.
por_opcion.to: Incorrect: to would give the final level (prices became 3%), which makes no sense here.

ejercicios.frase: The central bank rose interest rates again.
respuestas: The central bank raised interest rates again.
ejercicios.explicacion: The note on rise and raise applies: raise is transitive and takes a direct object; rise does not. The clue is interest rates, the direct object of the action, and the subject, the central bank, which acts on it. So the verb is raised. With rates as the subject you would say “interest rates rose”.
ejercicios.traduccion: El banco central volvió a subir los tipos de interés.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The central bank rose interest rates again.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: rose is intransitive and cannot take a direct object.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The central bank risen interest rates again.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Risen is the past participle of rise, which is intransitive, and the auxiliary is also missing; the right form is raised.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The central bank rised interest rates again.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Rised doesn't exist; with an object the verb is raise, raised.

ejercicios.frase: After a sharp rise, prices levelled ___ in the summer.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table includes level off / stabilise: to stop rising or falling after a rise or fall. It is a phrasal verb: level (to make flat) + off. The clue is the contrast with “a sharp rise”: after the sudden movement, the curve flattens out. Both off and out are accepted, because level out is a variant with the same meaning.
ejercicios.traduccion: Tras una fuerte subida, los precios se estabilizaron en verano.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Level up means to go up a level (in games or skills); it does not mean to stabilise.
Level down means to make things equal at a lower level; it does not mean to stabilise.
Spelling confusion between of and off; the particle is off.

ejercicios.frase: Interest rates went from 2% to 3%: a rise of one percentage ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: The warning in Rules and keys applies: do not confuse percent (porcentaje) with percentage point (punto porcentual). The difference between two percentages is measured in points: from 2% to 3% is one percentage point, whereas in relative terms the rise is 50%. The clue is percentage just before the gap.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The difference between two percentages is measured in percentage points.
ejercicios.traduccion: Los tipos de interés pasaron del 2 % al 3 %: una subida de un punto porcentual.

por_opcion.point: Correct: percentage point, the absolute difference between two percentages.
por_opcion.percent: Incorrect: “one percentage percent” doesn't exist; and saying it rose by 1% would be false, because in relative terms it rose by 50%.
por_opcion.per cent: Incorrect: it is the British spelling of percent and has the same problem.
por_opcion.number: Incorrect: percentage number is not an English expression.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with a verb (to reach a peak), in the past.
ejercicios.frase: Inflation ___ at 10% in October and then started to fall.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table includes peak / reach a peak, to reach the highest point, with the example “Inflation peaked at 10.8%”. Peak works as an intransitive verb and the level is introduced with at. The clue is the sequence: it reaches 10% and then starts to fall, so that was the highest point. The instruction asks for the past: peaked.
ejercicios.traduccion: La inflación alcanzó un máximo del 10 % en octubre y luego empezó a bajar.

errores_previstos.explicacion: The instruction asks for the past and the sentence narrates October: peaked.
Pick up means to recover, and it is also spelt and pronounced differently; to reach the highest point is peak.
Top exists with this meaning, but it is used without at (topped 10%); with at and the meaning of highest point, peaked.

ejercicios.frase: Shares ___ by 40% in a single day after the scandal.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table includes plunge / plummet / slump: to fall suddenly and steeply. The clue is the size and the cause: 40% in a single day after a scandal is a drastic fall. Plummeted is the most expressive verb in the list and, since it is intransitive, it fits with by 40%.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: A sharp fall after a scandal: “plummeted”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Las acciones se desplomaron un 40 % en un solo día tras el escándalo.

por_opcion.plummeted: Correct: they collapsed, a sudden and severe fall.
por_opcion.levelled off: Incorrect: it means to stabilise; it doesn't fit a 40% change or a scandal.
por_opcion.picked up: Incorrect: it means to recover, to go up; the opposite of what a scandal causes.
por_opcion.doubled: Incorrect: to double is to rise by 100%, and it is not combined with by 40%.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with an adjective (sudden and large).
ejercicios.frase: There has been a ___ rise in the price of olive oil.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table includes a sharp / steep rise: a sudden, large rise. Adjectives of intensity go before the noun rise. The clue is the gloss in the instruction (sudden and large). Sharp, steep and dramatic are accepted, because all three express a large, fast change; dramatic corresponds to the adverb dramatically in the table.
ejercicios.traduccion: Ha habido una subida brusca del precio del aceite de oliva.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Brusque exists, but it describes a person who is curt; for a rise you use sharp or steep.
Sharply is an adverb and goes with the verb (rose sharply); before the noun rise you need the adjective sharp.
Sharpen is a verb (to make sharper); before the noun rise you need the adjective sharp.

ejercicios.enunciado: Rewrite using the noun: start with “There was a”.
respuestas: There was a slight fall in exports in March.
There was a slight drop in exports in March.
There was a slight decline in exports in March.
There was a slight decrease in exports in March.
ejercicios.explicacion: The correspondence between verb + adverb and adjective + noun shown in the table applies: fell slightly becomes a slight fall. The quantity that changes is introduced with in (a fall in exports). Fall, drop, decline and decrease are accepted because all four also work as nouns with the same meaning.
ejercicios.traduccion: En marzo hubo una ligera caída de las exportaciones.

errores_previstos.respuesta: There was a slightly fall in exports in March.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Before a noun you need the adjective slight, not the adverb slightly.

errores_previstos.respuesta: There was a slight fall of exports in March.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The quantity that changes is introduced with in: a fall in exports.

errores_previstos.respuesta: There was a slight fell in exports in March.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Fell is the past of the verb; the noun is fall.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with a verb (to be reduced by half), as a past participle.
ejercicios.frase: The number of smokers has ___ since 2000.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table includes to halve, to be reduced by half, together with double and triple. The clue is has + past participle (present perfect, with since 2000) and the gloss in the instruction. Halve is regular: halved. Notice that the verb is halve (with v), different from the noun half.
ejercicios.traduccion: El número de fumadores se ha reducido a la mitad desde el año 2000.

errores_previstos.explicacion: The verb is halve, with v: halved. Half is the noun.
Halve already means to reduce by half; it takes no particle.
It is understandable, but it needs more words and the instruction asks for a single verb: halved.

ejercicios.frase: Rents in Madrid are twice as ___ as in Zaragoza.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table includes twice as high as, two times the amount of. The structure of multiplicative comparison is multiplier + as + adjective in the base form + as. The clue is the first as, already written: it forces you to use the base adjective, high, not the comparative.
ejercicios.traduccion: Los alquileres en Madrid son el doble de altos que en Zaragoza.

por_opcion.high: Correct: as + base adjective + as, preceded by the multiplier twice.
por_opcion.higher: Incorrect: the comparative goes with than (twice higher than is heard, but it is considered careless); with as… as you use the base adjective.
por_opcion.more high: Incorrect: high forms its comparative with -er; more high doesn't exist, and a comparative isn't needed here anyway.
por_opcion.highest: Incorrect: the superlative doesn't fit in a comparison between two items.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with one word (compared with the same period of the previous year).
ejercicios.explicacion: The table includes year-on-year (es: interanual), that is, compared with the same period of the previous year. It is a fixed expression with hyphens: year-on-year. The clue is the structure already started, year-on-, which can only be completed by repeating year. Its parallel is month-on-month.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Year-on-year” = compared with the same period last year (es: interanual).
ejercicios.traduccion: Las ventas minoristas crecieron un 3 % interanual.

errores_previstos.explicacion: The fixed expression is singular: year-on-year.
Annual means yearly, but it is not part of this expression; year is repeated.

ejercicios.explicacion: The rule on prepositions in this sheet and the typical mistake “increased in 2%” apply: the amount of the change is introduced with by, not with in. The version without a preposition (grew 5%), very common in the press, is also accepted. In is a literal translation of Spanish “crecieron en un 5 %”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The amount of the change is introduced with “by”, not “in”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Las exportaciones crecieron un 5 % el año pasado.

errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: the amount of the change goes with by.
To would give the final level (they became 5%), not the growth, which changes the meaning.
Of goes with the noun (growth of 5%), not with the verb.

respuestas: The rate held steady at two percent
ejercicios.explicacion: The table includes to remain stable / to hold steady, to stay at the same level, with the example “The rate held steady at 2%”. The order is subject (the rate) + verb (held) + adjective (steady) + at + level. The preposition at introduces the level at which it stays, just as with peak at.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Hold steady at” = to stay stable at a level.
ejercicios.traduccion: La tasa se mantuvo estable en el dos por ciento.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The rate held at two percent steady
errores_previstos.explicacion: Steady goes directly with the verb held: held steady at.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The rate steady held at two percent
errores_previstos.explicacion: The verb held goes before the adjective steady.

descripcion_larga_es: Verbs, nouns, adjectives and adverbs for describing graphs and data: rises, falls, stability, highs, lows, percentages and percentage points. It is the basic vocabulary of any economic report and of the financial press, essential for an economist. It is hard for Spanish speakers because of the prepositions (by versus to), the pair rise/raise and the difference between percent and percentage point.

contexto.que_es: It is the vocabulary for describing how a quantity changes over time: verbs for going up (rise, soar, pick up), going down (fall, plummet), stability (level off, hold steady), highs and lows (peak, bottom out), intensity modifiers (sharp, slight, dramatically) and expressions of comparison and approximation (twice as high as, just under).
contexto.por_que_importa: It is the everyday language of reports, press releases, central banks and international organisations, and it comes up in any presentation on economics. A wrong preposition changes the figure: “rose by 5%” and “rose to 5%” say different things. Confusing percent and percentage point is a serious conceptual error for an economist, and the pair rise/raise is an exam classic.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: When commenting on a graph, presenting statistics, summarising an economic outlook report or comparing data across periods. The signals are figures, dates and verbs of movement. Spanish speakers tend to use in for the amount (“increased in 2%”), until for the final level, raise without an object and a decimal comma.
